# Bridges (arch, truss, suspension) (`arch_bridge_truss`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by lever_mechanics_statics, geometry_proof, hydraulic_cement, lime_burning
- Core idea: A well-shaped masonry arch carries its load mainly in compression and so can be built of stone without tension, but it pushes outward and needs strong abutments and a temporary timber centring until the keystone is set; a flatter segmental arch (Zhaozhou, Ponte Vecchio) spans further with fewer piers, and open spandrels save weight and let floods through. A truss is a frame of triangles, which cannot deform without a member changing length, so timber or iron bars make long, light spans. A suspension bridge hangs the deck from cables or chains in tension anchored at both ends.
- Pitfalls:
  - Removing the centring before the mortar has set or before the arch is complete
  - Narrow piers with no protection against floods and scour (the commonest cause of collapse)
  - Rectangular timber frames without diagonals; they rack and fail
  - Light suspension decks in wind; they can oscillate and tear apart (Tacoma Narrows 1940)
- History: rome: 62 BC – Pons Fabricius, Rome; c. 106 AD Alcántara; china: c. 595–605 – Li Chun's Zhaozhou bridge, open-spandrel segmental arch of 37 m; iron chain suspension bridges by the Ming; americas: 15th c. – Inca grass-rope suspension bridges; europe: 1345 – Ponte Vecchio, Florence; 1567–69 Ponte Santa Trinita (Ammannati); 1570 Palladio's timber trusses; 1779 Iron Bridge, Coalbrookdale; 1826 Telford's Menai suspension bridge; 1883 Brooklyn Bridge
- Read:
  - Andrea Palladio, I quattro libri dell'architettura (1570), book III
  - David P. Billington, The Tower and the Bridge: The New Art of Structural Engineering (1983)
